children: “Practical men, who believe themselves to be quite exempt from any intellectual influence, are usually the slaves of some defunct economist.” So wrote the British economist John Maynard Keynes nearly a century ago, deploying one of his trademark literary zingers. “The Standard of Living”, a new play by James Graham currently showing to packed-out audiences in London’s West End, is a theatrical rendering of his maxim’s enduring truth.

Graham, whose previous plays portrayed Gareth Southgate, the manager of England’s soccer team, and media mogul Rupert Murdoch’s arrival on Fleet Street, has plenty of material to work with. Keynes, who died in 1946, was one of the most famous national figures in the political and economic spheres between the first and second world wars. But his friendships with the writer Virginia Woolf and other artists of the so-called “Bloomsbury set” made him a practitioner of the dismal science with an unusual focus on aesthetics, beauty and truth. This underpinned his preoccupation with identifying the components of a good life and how people can live better together.

Keynes’ marriage to a Russian ballerina, despite a previous preference for male partners, provides ample dramatic fodder. So does his gift for sharp-tongued public putdowns. His speculative trading gains and losses, meanwhile, would make a modern-day hedge fund manager blush.

Still, the heart of the play is a series of real and imagined exchanges between Keynes and his near-contemporary Friedrich Hayek. In economic theory, the pair are bookends. At one extreme the Austrian economist, scarred by his first-hand experience of 1920s hyperinflation in his home country, advocates the purging of periods of economic excess via cyclical recessions, sound government finances, and treating an undistorted price mechanism as sacrosanct. At the other Keynes, animated instead by the waste and misery of sky-high UK unemployment in the 1920s and 1930s, argued that governments should prioritise maintaining aggregate demand – if necessary, by running up deficits.

While the influence of the two camps waxed and waned over the subsequent century, their rival approaches continue to shape public policy. The Covid-era bailouts in the United States, Europe and elsewhere were Keynesian responses, even if the man himself envisaged intervention to deal with a slump in demand rather than supply. Bank bailouts during the 2008 Global Financial Crisis also had a Keynesian logic. Without those and other emergency measures, the world might have experienced a modern-day version of the Great Depression of the 1930s.

Although Hayek is firmly identified as the antagonist, replete with the economist’s familiar dismal outlook, Graham smartly avoids making him a pantomime villain. The Austrian’s influence was clear in the policies of British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s, and in the post-2008 shift to austerity in the United Kingdom and euro zone. Yet his critiques of Keynes retain their relevance. Careless interventions can spur inflation and have left governments in the developed world with uncomfortably high levels of debt. The decade of hyper-low interest rates that followed 2008, and European reluctance to tackle bank bad debts, was the opposite of Hayek’s preference for purging economic rot and probably contributed to anaemic growth across the continent.

Given his play is about the ongoing back-and-forth between the two theories, it’s apt that Graham finds inventive theatrical ways for Hayek and Keynes to interact – not least by literally dancing with each other. He also shows them locked in debate while serving as air raid wardens in Cambridge in 1942 – a meeting which actually took place. What “The Standard of Living” doesn’t do is conclude decisively who was right. The debate over the best approach towards economic management remains far from defunct.
Follow George Hay on Bluesky and LinkedIn.
“The Standard of Living”, by James Graham, is showing at the Theatre Royal Haymarket, London, until December 12.
